client: I've been really struggling lately with everything piling up at work — my boss just dumped two new projects on me with these insane deadlines, and I honestly don't know how I'm supposed to get it all done. It feels like no matter how hard I try, there's always more being added to my plate, and I'm starting to dread going in every morning. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because at the end of the day, the work is still going to be there.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now, and that dread in the mornings makes complete sense when you feel like you're running just to stay in place. I also hear a little skepticism about whether talking helps — and that's actually worth honoring, because you're right that our conversation won't make the deadlines disappear. What I'm curious about, though, is whether some of what's making this feel *impossible* might be the story you're telling yourself about it — so I'd love to ask: when you imagine not getting it all done, what do you fear will actually happen?

client: Honestly, my biggest fear is that my boss will see me as incompetent — like, that this will be the moment he finally realizes I can't handle the pressure and starts questioning why he even gave me these projects in the first place. There's also this nagging feeling that if I drop the ball, it'll affect my whole team and I'll have let everyone down. I know that might sound a bit extreme, but it feels very real when I'm lying awake at 2am thinking about it.
therapist: Those fears feel very real and valid — the weight of not wanting to disappoint your boss or your team says a lot about how much you care about your work and the people around you. I'm gently curious, though, about that thought "he'll finally realize I can't handle it" — the word *finally* caught my attention, as if part of you believes this moment has been coming for a while. What evidence do you actually have, from your history with this boss, about how he sees your competence?

client: I mean, if I'm being honest, he's actually given me positive feedback pretty consistently — he even told me last month that I was one of the more reliable people on the team. But somehow that doesn't really stick when I'm in the middle of a panic spiral, and I find myself thinking that maybe he was just being nice or didn't have the full picture yet. It's weird that I can know something logically and still not believe it when it counts.
therapist: What you just described — knowing something logically but not being able to *feel* it as true under stress — is actually one of the most common and frustrating patterns in anxiety, and it even has a name in CBT: we call it "discounting the positive," where your mind finds ways to explain away evidence that doesn't fit the fear. The fact that you can notice this happening, even from inside the spiral, is actually a real skill. I'm wondering — if a close friend came to you with the same track record of consistent praise and told you "he was probably just being nice," what would you say to them?

client: I'd probably tell them that the praise was genuine and they should trust it, that one difficult stretch doesn't erase a whole track record of good work. But when I try to turn that same logic on myself, it feels different — like the rules are somehow different for me, which I know doesn't really make sense when I say it out loud. I guess I'm just not sure how to actually make myself believe it in the moment when the anxiety kicks in, because it's easy to be rational now but a completely different thing at 2am.
therapist: You just caught something really important — that you're applying a harsher, more unforgiving standard to yourself than you would to anyone you care about, and hearing yourself say it out loud seemed to land differently. That gap between "rational now" and "2am spiral" is real, but one thing that can help is building that kinder voice *before* the anxiety peaks — almost like leaving yourself a note from this clearer-headed version of you. What do you think it would feel like to write down what you just said, so that the 2am version of you has something concrete to hold onto?

client: The idea actually makes some sense to me, but I'm a little skeptical that I'd even think to look at it when I'm in that state — like, when the anxiety is really bad, it's hard to imagine wanting to reach for something rational. There's also a part of me that worries I'd just read it and find a way to argue against it, the way I did just now with my boss's praise. I don't want to put in the effort and then have it just not work.
therapist: Your skepticism is really wise here — you're not just resisting the idea, you're actually identifying exactly how your mind works under stress, which is valuable self-knowledge. Rather than framing it as something that has to *convince* you in the moment, what if the note's job wasn't to win an argument with your anxious mind, but just to slow it down slightly — even 10 seconds of pause can interrupt a spiral enough to matter. Would you be open to treating it as a small experiment just once, not as a solution you have to believe in, but simply to see what actually happens?

client: Framing it as an experiment rather than something I have to fully believe in does make it feel a bit less daunting, I'll admit. I think my resistance comes from this all-or-nothing thinking where if it doesn't completely fix the anxiety, it's a failure — so redefining what "working" even means helps a little. I guess I could try writing something down tonight, though I'm still not fully convinced, and part of me is already bracing for the version of myself that reads it and just rolls my eyes at it.
therapist: It's actually a really good sign that you can already picture the eye-rolling version of yourself — that means you're going in with realistic expectations rather than setting yourself up for disappointment, which is much healthier than all-or-nothing thinking. And honestly, even if you do roll your eyes, you'll have learned something true about what you need in that moment, which is still useful data from the experiment. When you imagine sitting down tonight to write it, what feels like the most important thing your 2am self actually needs to hear?

client: I think the most important thing my 2am self needs to hear is that one hard stretch at work doesn't define my whole career or who I am as a person — and that my boss's consistent praise is real evidence, not just politeness. But even as I say that, I notice I'm already mentally drafting counterarguments, like "but this time the stakes are higher" or "but you've never had two projects at once before." I guess that's exactly the pattern you've been pointing to, and it's a little unsettling to watch my own mind do it in real time.
therapist: Watching your own mind generate those counterarguments in real time like that is actually a significant moment — it's the difference between being *inside* the spiral and being able to *observe* it, and that observer part of you is exactly what CBT tries to strengthen. Those counterarguments ("but this time is different") are worth writing down too, not to defeat them, but so your 2am self can see them coming and recognize them as familiar patterns rather than new evidence. I'm curious — now that you've caught your mind doing this live, does it change anything about how much authority you want to give those counterarguments?

client: It does shift something slightly, yeah — like, seeing it happen in real time makes it harder to fully trust those counterarguments as objective truth, because I can see they're just my anxiety being creative rather than actual evidence. But I'm also a bit worried that knowing this intellectually won't translate into anything useful when I'm exhausted and stressed at 2am, because right now I feel relatively calm and it's easy to be the observer. I suppose that's exactly why you're suggesting I write it down while I'm in this clearer headspace, which I can see the logic in even if I'm not totally confident it'll hold up under pressure.
therapist: You've just done something really meaningful in this conversation — you've moved from "I don't know if talking will change anything" to genuinely understanding *why* the writing exercise might help, even while holding onto healthy skepticism about it, and that shift matters more than you might realize. The gap between knowing and feeling in the moment is real, and we're not trying to close it all at once — we're just trying to leave a small handhold for your exhausted 2am self to grab onto. So as you think about writing that note tonight, what feels like one honest, specific sentence you could put down that even your most anxious self might find hard to completely dismiss?

client: Maybe something like: "Last month your boss specifically said you're one of the most reliable people on the team, and that was true then and it's still true now." That feels harder to argue with because it's a specific, concrete thing that actually happened rather than a general reassurance I could dismiss as wishful thinking. I'm still a little nervous about whether I'll actually follow through with writing it tonight, because there's a part of me that will probably feel silly doing it, but I think I can push past that.
therapist: That sentence is really strong — it's specific, it's grounded in reality, and you came up with it yourself, which means it carries more weight than anything I could have handed you. The "feeling silly" part is worth naming too, because sometimes that feeling is just resistance showing up in a different costume, and pushing through it anyway is actually part of the experiment. What would it mean for you if you did follow through tonight — not whether it works perfectly, but just the act of doing it for yourself?

client: I think it would mean that I'm actually taking my own anxiety seriously enough to do something about it, rather than just white-knuckling through and hoping the dread goes away on its own. There's something almost uncomfortable about that, like it requires admitting that I need to be taken care of in a way I'm not totally used to doing for myself. I guess I've spent so long just pushing through that the idea of actively trying to help myself feels unfamiliar, almost indulgent — which probably says something I should think about.
therapist: What you just named — that caring for yourself feels "indulgent" — is such an important thread to pull on, because it suggests you may have learned somewhere along the way that your needs are less deserving of attention than just powering through, and that belief might be quietly fueling a lot of the pressure you put on yourself. Writing that note tonight isn't indulgence — it's actually the same care and logic you'd offer a struggling friend without hesitation. I'm wondering, where do you think that idea came from — that taking care of yourself is something you have to earn or justify?
